    How to be a great manager

    Five essentials to highlight before our session, in about 10 minutes.

    Hey! Before we meet, I'll show you what great managers do. It takes about 10 minutes.

    Agenda

    1Think and act like a great manager.
    2Make accountability meaningful.
    3Delegate outcomes, not tasks.
    4Give feedback with the SBI model.
    5Set SMART goals your team can reach.
    There are only 5 things and I assure you they make a difference.

    Step 1: How to be a great manager

    From star player to team leader

    You were probably promoted for being great at the work. Now the job is different: your success comes from your team's results.
    Your success is now measured by your team's results.

    We delve deeper

    3 ways to equip yourself for success

    1.Own the identity shift
    ↻
    See yourself and your success differently. Ask: how can I help my team get better results?
    ↻
    2.Manage yourself first
    ↻
    Your team takes its cues from you. Stay calm when bad news arrives and get the full story before you react.
    ↻
    3.Build your support network
    ↻
    Find mentors and sounding boards inside or outside the company. Don't lean on your team for this: they need you.
    ↻
    Flip each card. If you do this… you start strong!

    Step 2: Accountability

    Clear goals, clear owners, regular check-ins

    What it means

    Knowing who is responsible for a deliverable and making sure it gets done thoroughly and well. It rests on clear goals that you and your team member agree on together.

    Who owns it? By when? How will we know it's done?

    We delve deeper

    How a team reaches mutual accountability

    As the leader, you set the tone and create psychological safety. Teams climb these steps in order (Lencioni's model).

    1Trust
    2Healthy conflict
    3Commitment
    4Mutual accountability
    5High performance
    Team accountability starts with trust.

    Step 3: Delegation

    Delegate outcomes, not tasks

    Delegation means transferring ownership, not passing on tasks to save time. Share the purpose, the result you want and the authority to decide.
    Tell them what success looks like, then step back.

    The 5 levels of delegation

    Choose how much control to keep

    Level 1Do exactly what I say
    ↻
    For new, complex or zero-error tasks. Don't stay here long.
    ↻
    Level 2Research and report back
    ↻
    They gather the facts and bring them to you. You still decide.
    ↻
    Level 3Recommend, then act with approval
    ↻
    Define the outcome and the boundaries. They plan, you approve.
    ↻
    Level 4Decide and inform
    ↻
    For highly skilled people. They own it and keep you informed.
    ↻
    Level 5Full ownership
    ↻
    Built on trust. They hold full authority for the result.
    ↻

    Tap each card. Check in more often at first, then taper off as confidence grows. Model by Michael Hyatt, featured in the ATD article.

    Match the level to the person and the risk.

    Hand off, then let go

    Build readiness step by step

    Hand off responsibility, then let go of authority. Done well, it frees your time for strategy: seeing around the corner.

    Stage 1

    "Come and watch me do it."

    Stage 2

    "Let's do it together. You help me."

    Stage 3

    "Let's do it together. I watch you."

    Stage 4

    "You do it. I'm here to support."

    You choose to delegate. It never happens by chance.

    Step 4: Feedback with SBI

    Specific, factual and useful

    S
    Situation
    ↻
    When and where did it happen? Name the specific time and place to avoid confusion.
    ↻
    B
    Behavior
    ↻
    What did the person do or say? Observable facts only, no opinions or judgments.
    ↻
    I
    Impact
    ↻
    What was the result? Share the effect on you, the team or the client, positive or negative.
    ↻

    Tap each card to reveal what it means.

    Facts first. No labels, no judgments.

    SBI in action

    Use it for praise and for improvement

    Example

    S

    Situation"In yesterday's client call,

    B

    Behavioryou summarized the agreed actions and owners before we closed.

    I

    ImpactThe client wrote back that it was the clearest call we've had. Thank you."

    SBI works for praise too!

    Step 5: SMART goals

    Goals your team can see, track and reach

    S
    Specific
    ↻
    What exactly will be done, and by whom?
    ↻
    M
    Measurable
    ↻
    Which number or criteria will show progress?
    ↻
    A
    Achievable
    ↻
    A stretch, but realistic with your resources.
    ↻
    R
    Relevant
    ↻
    Linked to team and business priorities.
    ↻
    T
    Time-bound
    ↻
    A clear deadline, with milestones on the way.
    ↻
    If you can't track it, you can't reach it.

    We delve deeper

    4 steps to achieve your team's goals

    1.Lock on your target
    ↻
    Focus on the 3 or 4 results that matter most. Agree priorities with stakeholders.
    ↻
    2.Build your system
    ↻
    Break big goals into short-term targets. Track them in weekly plans, 1:1s and team meetings.
    ↻
    3.Rally your team
    ↻
    Ask the team to help design the system, new members included.
    ↻
    4.Structure to win
    ↻
    Put the routine in the team calendar. Keep to the timeline and your commitments.
    ↻
    People support what they help create.

    Your role as manager

    • Meet each team member regularly to guide, support and recognize them.
    • Give constructive feedback on performance.
    • Model the values you expect from others.
    • Hold people accountable as individuals and as a team.
    Delegating a task
    Delegating an outcome
    "Update the weekly report."
    "Update the weekly report so leadership can spot gaps in the data."
    They complete the task, but may not flag missing or outdated figures.
    They know what success looks like, so they check the data and raise gaps.
    1

    Giving the task without the purpose or the result you want.

    2

    Not defining what good looks like: quality, deadline, metric or limits.

    3

    Not clarifying authority: should they execute, recommend, decide or own it?

    4

    Checking in too much (signals no trust) or too little (small issues grow).

    Competence

    Can they do this assignment?

    Bandwidth

    Do they have the time to do it?

    Drive

    Will they see it through to the end?

    Fit

    Will they work well with others while doing it?

    4 questions to choose who is ready for a stretch assignment

    Make it a two-way conversation

    • Ask about intent: "What were you hoping to achieve?" Then compare intent with impact.
    • Agree on next steps and how you'll follow up on progress.
    • Give feedback often, not only at review time.
    • It may feel awkward at first. It gets easier with practice.
